analysis.one_liner: Strips arrests, juvenile records, and old convictions from tenant background reports.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal credit-reporting law for tenant screening. Consumer reporting agencies could no longer put arrests, juvenile records, dismissed or diverted cases, completed sentences, court-fee debts, or pardoned convictions on reports used to screen renters, and convictions of any kind would drop off after seven years. Landlords who reject an applicant based on the report would have to say exactly why, in writing, within three days. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters with a past in the criminal legal system. People with an arrest that never led to a conviction, a juvenile record, a sentence they finished, or a pardon could no longer be screened out by those records on a tenant report. People who owe court fees or incarceration-related debts could no longer have those debts block a rental. Because arrest and conviction records fall heavily on Black and Latino Americans, the bill would remove a barrier that falls hardest on those groups.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters with criminal or court-debt records

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits consumer reporting agencies from including arrests, juvenile adjudications or convictions, resolved criminal cases, completed sentences, court-fee and incarceration-related debts, expunged or pardoned records on tenant screening reports [S2][S3].
Excludes criminal convictions older than seven years from all consumer reports by removing the conviction exception to the FCRA's seven-year limit [S2][S3].
Requires anyone taking an adverse action, such as denying a rental, based on a tenant screening report to give the consumer a copy of the report and the specific reasons within three days [S2][S3].
Requires consumer reporting agencies, on request, to tell the consumer which entity supplied information on their report [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and tenant screening companies, who would lose access to criminal-record and court-debt data they now use to reject applicants. Screening firms would lose reportable data to sell; landlords would have less information about an applicant's recent history. A fair-minded reader should also weigh the concern of landlords and neighbors that recent serious offenses would no longer be visible to them.

drawbacks.text: The bill would bar even very recent serious convictions from tenant reports: it excludes any conviction for which the applicant is still on probation or parole [S3].

A preemption provision would stop states from setting their own time limits on when reportable information becomes obsolete, taking away the ability of states to write stricter rules than the federal seven-year cap [S3].

Landlord and screening-industry groups argue that hiding criminal records from tenant reports forces landlords to guess, raises insurance and liability concerns, and pushes screening toward other criteria that can also disadvantage applicants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a completed sentence, an arrest without conviction, or a court-fee debt is a poor predictor of being a good tenant, and these records currently keep many people from housing indefinitely. The honest cost is on the other side of the ledger: a landlord who wants to know about a conviction from last year would no longer be able to see it, and the state preemption clause takes choices away from states that wrote tougher rules. The bill is a genuine trade-off, weighted toward giving people with records a second chance at housing.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, with 16 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tenant screening companies and landlords are better off, because they keep the current system in which criminal records, juvenile records, and court-fee debts appear on tenant reports and can be used to reject applicants. People with those records remain shut out of housing by the same barriers the bill would have removed.

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip criminal-record and court-debt information from tenant screening reports.

against.name: Rep. Patrick McHenry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter named in the record was a Democrat (16 cosponsors plus the sponsor), no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Tenant screening and consumer reporting agencies
industries.note: These firms make money furnishing criminal, juvenile, and court-debt records for tenant screening; the bill would forbid much of that data from tenant reports and cap reportable convictions at seven years. Their revenue interest in more reportable data runs against renters' interest in getting housing with an old record.

Landlords would lose access to criminal-record and court-debt information when picking tenants, and would face new written notice duties when rejecting applicants. Some landlords gain too, since screening out people with records shrinks their applicant pool and leaves units empty longer.
